title: Actually, Zara Larsson Isn’t Eligible For Best New Artist. She’s Already a Grammy Nominee
summary: Larsson said she didn't want to submit for the category in an interview circulating the internet. But she can't — here's why
whatHappening: Zara Larsson recently stated she didn't want to submit for the Grammy Award for Best New Artist, but she's ineligible anyway due to her prior Grammy nomination history. The Swedish singer cannot compete in the category regardless of her personal preference.
whoInvolved: Zara Larsson is a Swedish singer and songwriter who rose to prominence in 2008 after winning the second season of the Swedish talent show Talang. She has released multiple studio albums and charted singles since her 2012 signing with Ten Music Group.
whyMatters: The situation highlights how the Best New Artist eligibility criteria work in practice, beyond what artists may assume or publicly state. For emerging artists and industry observers, understanding these hard rules prevents confusion about Grammy qualification and ensures only truly eligible artists are considered for the award.
articleBody:
Zara Larsson may have said she didn't want to submit for the Best New Artist category at the Grammy Awards, but the Swedish singer wouldn't be able to compete regardless. According to Rolling Stone, while Larsson expressed her preference not to enter the category in a recent interview circulating online, she is actually ineligible due to her prior Grammy nomination history.

The Best New Artist award, presented annually since the 2nd Grammy Awards in 1960, is specifically designated "for a new artist who releases, during the Eligibility Year, the first recording which establishes the public identity of that artist." This definition is stricter than many assume—it's not merely about being new to the music industry broadly, but rather about having a first commercial recording that established public recognition. Once an artist has already earned a Grammy nomination, they have crossed the threshold of public identity establishment and can no longer qualify.

Larsson first rose to prominence in 2008 after winning the second season of the Swedish talent show competition Talang. She signed with Ten Music Group in 2012 and released her debut extended play, Introducing, the following year. Her single "Uncover" became a massive hit, charting at number one in Sweden—where it was certified six-times platinum—and in Norway. By the time her debut studio album 1 arrived in 2014, she had already established herself as a significant recording artist with charted singles like "Carry You Home."

Given her earlier Grammy nominations, Larsson's eligibility window for Best New Artist closed long ago. The category's definition means that public recognition, whether through chart success, award nominations, or industry acknowledgment, determines ineligibility. While Larsson's recent comments about not submitting may reflect her current preferences about award submissions, the Grammy eligibility rules themselves would have already excluded her from consideration.

The distinction matters because it demonstrates how the Grammys enforce their eligibility criteria based on objective career milestones rather than artist choice or timing of submissions. For artists and their teams navigating Grammy eligibility, understanding these technical rules is essential.

title: Dolly Parton’s Sister Stella Honors Singer: ‘Dolly Loved the World and Everyone in It’
summary: “My sister was one of the most generous, thoughtful, and kind people I’ve ever known,” she writes in online tribute
whatHappening: Stella Parton, the younger sister of country music icon Dolly Parton, has published an online tribute honoring the late singer. In her message, Stella describes Dolly as one of the most generous, thoughtful, and kind people she has known.
whoInvolved: Stella Mae Parton is an American country singer and songwriter who charted a series of country singles in the mid-to-late-1970s, with her biggest hit being "I Want to Hold You in My Dreams Tonight" in 1975. Dolly Parton, her older sister, was a Grammy and Emmy Award-winning country music legend known as the "Queen of Country" who sold over 100 million records and built a philanthropic legacy through Dollywood and the Dollywood Foundation.
whyMatters: Dolly Parton's death marks the end of an era for country music and popular culture, given her status as one of the most honored performers in history. Family tributes like Stella's offer intimate perspectives on Dolly's character beyond her public persona and career achievements, helping shape how her legacy is remembered by fans and the public.
articleBody:
Stella Parton is honoring her late sister Dolly Parton with a heartfelt online tribute, describing the country music icon as one of the most generous, thoughtful, and kind people she has ever known. According to Rolling Stone, Stella wrote that "Dolly loved the world and everyone in it," capturing what she saw as the essence of her older sister's character and worldview.

Dolly Parton, who died recently, was one of the most celebrated figures in American music history. Dubbed the "Queen of Country," she earned eleven Grammy Awards and three Emmy Awards throughout her career, along with nominations for two Academy Awards, six Golden Globes, and a Tony Award. With more than 100 million records sold, she stands among the best-selling music artists of all time.

Beyond her musical achievements, Dolly became equally renowned for her cultural influence and extensive philanthropic work. She founded Dollywood, the theme park in her native Tennessee, and established the Dollywood Foundation, which has supported countless charitable initiatives. Her generosity extended across education, healthcare, and community development, making her a figure of significance far beyond the recording industry.

Stella, herself an accomplished country musician, released a series of charting singles during the mid-to-late-1970s, with her most successful song being "I Want to Hold You in My Dreams Tonight" in 1975. As Dolly's younger sister, Stella was uniquely positioned to witness both the public triumphs and private character of the music legend. Her tribute underscores the personal dimensions of a woman the world knew primarily through her performances and philanthropy.

The loss of Dolly Parton represents a significant moment for country music and American popular culture. Her influence shaped generations of musicians and fans, while her business acumen and philanthropic vision established a template for celebrity engagement with social causes. Stella's words serve as a reminder that beneath the awards, records, and monuments to Dolly's success was a person defined by warmth and compassion toward others.

title: Jack Osbourne Says Upcoming Ozzy Movie Won’t Be an ‘Artsy, Esoteric Biopic’
summary: "I’m always saying in the meetings, ‘We’ve got to give the fans what they want,'" he confirmed
whatHappening: Jack Osbourne is weighing in on the upcoming Ozzy Osbourne biopic, insisting it will be a fan-focused film rather than an experimental or overly artistic take on his father's life. He's emphasizing that the filmmakers are committed to delivering what audiences actually want to see.
whoInvolved: Jack Osbourne, a British-American media personality and youngest child of Ozzy Osbourne, is involved in the project. Ozzy, the legendary heavy metal pioneer and co-founder of Black Sabbath, is the subject of the film. Jack has worked in entertainment and media since his days on MTV's reality series The Osbournes.
whyMatters: The approach to Ozzy's biopic signals how studios are balancing artistic ambition with audience expectations for music documentaries and biopics. Given Ozzy's iconic but controversial history—from his pioneering work with Black Sabbath to his well-documented personal struggles—the filmmaking choices will shape how his legacy is presented to both longtime fans and new generations.
articleBody:
Jack Osbourne is setting expectations for the forthcoming Ozzy Osbourne biopic, making clear that producers are prioritizing fan satisfaction over artistic experimentation. According to Rolling Stone, Jack has been vocal in production meetings about steering the film toward what audiences want rather than pursuing an esoteric or overly highbrow interpretation of his father's life story.

"I'm always saying in the meetings, 'We've got to give the fans what they want,'" Jack confirmed, underlining his role in advocating for an accessible, entertaining approach to the material.

Ozzy Osbourne, born John Michael Osbourne, stands as one of heavy metal's defining figures. Dubbed the "Prince of Darkness," he co-founded the legendary band Black Sabbath in 1968 and became the lead vocalist on their first eight studio albums throughout the 1970s, including landmark releases like Paranoid and Master of Reality. His firing from Black Sabbath in 1979 due to substance abuse problems marked a turning point that could easily become a focal point of any biopic—a moment of both personal crisis and professional reinvention.

Jack's insistence on delivering fan-friendly content reflects a broader strategy in music biography: avoiding the trap of self-conscious artistry that might alienate the very people most invested in Ozzy's story. The Osbourne family has long understood the power of direct fan engagement, beginning with their groundbreaking appearance on MTV's reality series The Osbournes, which ran from 2002 to 2005 and brought the family into living rooms across America.

The decision to keep the film grounded and entertaining rather than experimental suggests the producers are learning from both successful music biopics and missteps in the genre. Jack's involvement in these production conversations positions him as a bridge between the filmmakers and the fanbase—a role he's well-suited for given his experience in media and entertainment.

With the biopic still in development, Jack's comments provide insight into the creative philosophy guiding the project: authenticity and audience connection will take precedence over pretension.

articleBody:

title: Lil Durk Trial: Jurors See Unreleased ‘Redman’ Video, Defense Calls It ‘Expression of Art’
summary: At the rap star's murder-for-hire trial, his defense lawyer Brian Steel called him a poet who paints "pictures with words"
whatHappening: Jurors in Lil Durk's murder-for-hire trial have been shown an unreleased music video titled 'Redman.' The rapper's defense attorney is arguing the video represents artistic expression rather than evidence of criminal intent.
whoInvolved: Lil Durk (Durk Devontay Banks), a Chicago-based drill music pioneer and one of the subgenre's most commercially successful rappers, is on trial. His defense attorney is Brian Steel, an American criminal defense lawyer best known for representing Young Thug in Georgia's lengthy YSL racketeering trial.
whyMatters: The trial hinges partly on how jurors interpret Lil Durk's artistic output and whether creative content can be weaponized as evidence in criminal proceedings. The outcome could set precedent for how courts weigh rap lyrics and music videos in cases involving rappers accused of violence or conspiracy.
articleBody:
Jurors in the murder-for-hire trial of rapper Lil Durk have been presented with an unreleased music video for a track titled 'Redman,' sparking debate over the line between artistic expression and criminal evidence. According to Rolling Stone, Lil Durk's defense attorney Brian Steel argued that the video represents nothing more than the rapper's creative work, describing his client as a poet who paints 'pictures with words.'

Lil Durk, born Durk Devontay Banks, has built his career as a pioneering figure in Chicago drill music, a subgenre he helped popularize. His breakthrough came through the Signed to the Streets mixtape series released between 2013 and 2014, which led to a recording contract with Def Jam Recordings and subsequent studio albums including Remember My Name and Lil Durk 2X. The rapper has become one of drill music's most commercially successful artists, maintaining a prominent place in hip-hop for over a decade.

The introduction of the unreleased 'Redman' video into trial testimony reflects a broader prosecutorial strategy of using a defendant's creative output as potential evidence of motive, consciousness of guilt, or gang affiliation. Steel's characterization of Durk as a poet working within his artistic medium challenges this approach, positioning the video within the context of hip-hop's tradition of narrative storytelling and vivid imagery.

Brian Steel brings significant experience to the defense. He previously served as lead counsel for Young Thug in Georgia's YSL racketeering trial, which lasted over 22 months and became the longest trial in Georgia's history. That high-profile case involved similar questions about the relationship between rap lyrics, music videos, and criminal allegations—challenges that Steel navigated through a multi-year courtroom battle.

The trial's treatment of artistic evidence carries implications beyond this single case. Hip-hop artists and their legal representatives have long argued that rap music, like other genres, employs fictional narratives, exaggeration, and creative license. However, courts have sometimes treated rap lyrics and visual content differently than they might treat other artistic mediums, a disparity that civil rights advocates have criticized as discriminatory. The jury's response to Steel's 'expression of art' defense will signal how seriously this particular court weighs that argument.

articleBody:

Parton, who earned the title "Queen of Country," built one of the most decorated careers in music history. The musician's appearance guest-hosting the program provided an opportunity to reflect on Parton's impact at a moment when her passing has prompted broader conversations about her place in American cultural history. title: Paul McCartney and John Lennon Crack Each Other Up in Rare ‘Day Tripper’ Demo
summary: The "Songwriting Work Tape" version of the classic single was recorded at Lennon's house and will be included on the upcoming special edition of Rubber Soul
whatHappening: A rare demo recording of the Beatles' "Day Tripper" is surfacing, capturing Paul McCartney and John Lennon joking and laughing together during a songwriting session at Lennon's house. The "Songwriting Work Tape" version will be included on an upcoming special edition of Rubber Soul.
whoInvolved: Paul McCartney and John Lennon, the songwriting partnership behind the Beatles, one of the most influential rock bands in history. "Day Tripper" was primarily written by Lennon with contributions from McCartney and released as a double A-side single with "We Can Work It Out" in December 1965.
whyMatters: Unreleased demos and work tapes from the Beatles' recording sessions are rare archival finds that offer fans and historians intimate glimpses into the creative process of one of music's greatest songwriting duos. The release underscores the enduring commercial and cultural value of Beatles material, with new editions continuing to drive interest in their catalog decades after the band's breakup.
articleBody:
A candid demo recording of "Day Tripper" is being released for the first time, capturing an unguarded moment between Paul McCartney and John Lennon as they worked through the classic song. According to Rolling Stone, the "Songwriting Work Tape" version was recorded at Lennon's house and will appear on an upcoming special edition of Rubber Soul, the Beatles' sixth studio album from 1965. The tape preserves the two musicians laughing and cracking each other up, offering a rare window into their creative collaboration in the studio.

"Day Tripper" holds an important place in Beatles history. Released in December 1965 as a double A-side single paired with "We Can Work It Out," the track was primarily written by John Lennon with some contributions from Paul McCartney, credited to the Lennon–McCartney partnership. Both songs were recorded during the sessions for Rubber Soul, which was released on 3 December 1965 on EMI's Parlophone label in the United Kingdom. The single proved to be a commercial success, topping the charts in Britain, Ireland, the Netherlands, and Norway.

The emergence of this demo recording is significant for Beatles archivists and fans alike. Work tapes and informal studio recordings from the band's early years are exceedingly rare, as much of their recorded output from the 1960s was either officially released or has remained in private vaults. This particular tape is notable not only for its historical value but for the intimate quality it captures—the easy rapport between Lennon and McCartney as they composed, with moments of levity punctuating their creative process. Such artifacts provide context that finished recordings cannot offer, revealing the spontaneity and humor that characterized their songwriting sessions.

Rubber Soul itself was described as an important artistic achievement for the band upon its release, and it remains a landmark album in rock music history. The album's special edition will bring together previously unreleased material alongside the original recordings, appealing to both longtime collectors and new listeners discovering the Beatles' catalog. The inclusion of the "Day Tripper" work tape suggests a broader effort to document and preserve the band's creative legacy in ways that celebrate both the finished product and the human moments behind it.

whatHappening: Kesha has released a cover of Dolly Parton's 1980 hit 'Old Flames (Can't Hold a Candle to You)' as a tribute to the country music legend. The song carries special significance for Kesha, as it was co-written by her mother, Pebe Sebert.

articleBody:
Kesha has paid homage to one of country music's greatest icons by recording a cover of Dolly Parton's 1980 classic 'Old Flames (Can't Hold a Candle to You).' According to Rolling Stone, the tribute takes on added significance given that the song was co-written by Kesha's mother, Pebe Sebert, creating a deeply personal connection to the material for the artist.

Parton's original recording of the track became one of her signature songs during a career that would ultimately earn her recognition as the 'Queen of Country.' Over her decades in the music industry, Parton established herself as one of the most honored country performers in history, accumulating eleven Grammy Awards, three Emmy Awards, and nominations for two Academy Awards and a Tony Award, among numerous other accolades.

Kesha's decision to cover this particular song represents more than a simple tribute to a fellow performer. The inclusion of her mother as a co-writer links three generations of songwriting and performance talent, underscoring the deep roots of musical creativity within her family. Pebe Sebert's contributions to country music songwriting, though perhaps less publicly recognized than her daughter's pop stardom, established a creative legacy that now extends into Kesha's artistic journey.

For Kesha, the cover also reflects an evolution in her artistic identity. Having achieved chart success with albums like Animal (2010) and Rainbow (2017), along with major hits including 'Tik Tok' and collaborations such as 'Timber' with Pitbull, she has demonstrated her capacity to work across multiple musical genres and styles. The Parton cover adds another dimension to her versatility as a performer.

The tribute marks a moment of artistic intersection where contemporary pop and country music traditions meet, with Kesha honoring both Parton's enduring legacy and her own family's contribution to music history through her mother's songwriting work on this 1980 standard.

title: Watch Jack White’s Emotional Cover ‘Jolene’ in Honor of Dolly Parton

whatHappening: Jack White performed an emotional cover of 'Jolene' during a London concert as a tribute to Dolly Parton following her death. The rock musician's rendition honored the country legend and her enduring musical legacy.
whoInvolved: Jack White, the guitarist and lead vocalist of the White Stripes who built a successful solo career after the band's 2011 split, performed the tribute. Dolly Parton, the 'Queen of Country' and one of the most honored country performers in history with eleven Grammy Awards and numerous other accolades, passed away on Tuesday.
whyMatters: The performance underscores the cross-genre influence Parton wielded throughout her career, with major rock and pop artists recognizing her songwriting genius. White's public tribute during a live concert demonstrates how Parton's work transcended country music and shaped artists across musical boundaries, cementing her legacy beyond her genre.
articleBody:
Jack White took to the stage in London to deliver a poignant cover of 'Jolene,' Dolly Parton's most iconic song, in honor of the country music legend who died earlier this week. According to Rolling Stone, the musician performed the emotional rendition during his concert as a tribute to Parton following her passing on Tuesday. The performance marked a significant public acknowledgment of Parton's influence on musicians working across genres.

Dolly Parton, who earned the title 'Queen of Country,' was one of the most honored country performers in history. Over her legendary career, she accumulated eleven Grammy Awards, three Emmy Awards, the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award, and nominations for two Academy Awards, six Golden Globe Awards, and a Tony Award. Beyond her musical achievements, Parton became a cultural icon whose compositions and recordings touched audiences far beyond country music's traditional boundaries.

'Jolene,' one of Parton's most recognizable songs, became a standard covered by artists across multiple genres. The song's emotional vulnerability and universal themes made it a vehicle for tributes from performers who may not have recorded country music themselves. White's decision to perform the song in concert demonstrated how deeply Parton's work had penetrated rock and alternative music circles.

Jack White, who was the guitarist and lead vocalist of the rock duo the White Stripes, became a key figure in the 2000s indie and garage rock movements before launching a solo career following the band's 2011 split. His willingness to perform Parton's work underscored a broader respect among rock musicians for the country artist's songwriting craft and emotional depth. White's career has been marked by his distinctive musical techniques and eccentricity, qualities that perhaps gave him the artistic credibility to interpret one of country music's most delicate compositions.

Parton's death represents the loss of a major cultural figure whose influence extended across generational and genre lines. Artists like White, who might seem removed from country music's mainstream, felt compelled to honor her publicly, suggesting the depth of her legacy in popular music. The London concert tribute became a moment of collective recognition of Parton's immeasurable contributions to music and culture.

articleBody:
Gap Inc. is elevating its Encore membership program by hosting an exclusive performance by singer-songwriter Gigi Perez during New York Fashion Week on September 14. Performing at a Fashion Week event, even as part of a brand partnership, provides additional visibility and credibility as she continues to build on the success of "Sailor Song" and expand her presence beyond social media platforms that initially drove her popularity.

title: Jim James Tries to Get Found on New Solo Song ‘Lost Child’
summary: Track will appear on upcoming album, Wowed Out, due Friday
whatHappening: Jim James, the primary songwriter and vocalist of My Morning Jacket, has released a new solo song titled 'Lost Child.' The track will appear on his upcoming album, Wowed Out, arriving this Friday.
whoInvolved: Jim James (James Edward Olliges Jr.) is an American vocalist, guitarist, and producer best known as the primary songwriter of the rock band My Morning Jacket, formed in Louisville, Kentucky in 1998. My Morning Jacket is an experimental, psychedelic rock band that built a significant following beginning in the 2000s, partly through their acclaimed live performances.
whyMatters: The release signals continued solo activity from James alongside his work with My Morning Jacket, demonstrating his ongoing creative output across multiple projects. The album drop this Friday marks a notable moment for fans of both his solo work and the broader My Morning Jacket universe.
articleBody:
Jim James is stepping into the spotlight with a new solo single as his upcoming album approaches release. 'Lost Child,' according to Rolling Stone, will be featured on Wowed Out, an album set to arrive this Friday. The track represents James's latest foray into solo material, continuing a pattern of artistic expansion beyond his primary role in My Morning Jacket.

James, professionally known as Jim James or Yim Yames, has established himself as a multifaceted musician throughout his career. As the vocalist, guitarist, and primary songwriter of My Morning Jacket—the Louisville-based rock band he has anchored since its formation in 1998—James has helped shape the group's distinctive sound, which blends rock and country influences with experimental and psychedelic elements. The band, rounded out by bassist Tom Blankenship, drummer Patrick Hallahan, guitarist Carl Broemel, and keyboardist Bo Koster, built a devoted following beginning in the 2000s in part due to their reputation for dynamic live performances.

Beyond My Morning Jacket, James has also pursued a parallel solo career, releasing several albums that allow him to explore different creative directions. This solo work has given him space to develop his production skills and songwriting voice independently, complementing rather than competing with his responsibilities in the band. The forthcoming album Wowed Out appears to continue this tradition of independent artistic expression.

The release of 'Lost Child' comes as James prepares to share the full scope of Wowed Out with listeners this week. With the album's imminent arrival, the single serves as a preview of what fans can expect from his latest body of solo work. The track's title suggests themes of searching and displacement, potentially offering insight into the album's broader thematic concerns.

title: Johnny Marr Finds Defiance in Idealism on New Single ‘It’s Time’
summary: The Smiths guitarist will release his fifth solo album, The Age of Everything, in October
whatHappening: Johnny Marr, legendary guitarist of The Smiths, has released a new single titled 'It's Time' that showcases idealistic themes. The track arrives ahead of his fifth solo album, The Age of Everything, set for October release.
whoInvolved: Johnny Marr is an English-born Irish musician best known as guitarist and co-songwriter of The Smiths, the influential Manchester rock band active from 1982 to 1987. He has maintained a prolific solo career alongside work with numerous other bands since the group's split.
whyMatters: The release marks another significant milestone in Marr's solo trajectory and signals continued artistic evolution nearly four decades after The Smiths' original run. For fans of one of British rock's most important bands, new solo material demonstrates that Marr remains creatively engaged and willing to explore contemporary themes through his distinctive guitar work.
articleBody:
Johnny Marr continues to cement his solo legacy with the release of 'It's Time,' a new single that finds the storied guitarist channeling defiance through idealistic messaging. According to Rolling Stone, the track precedes Marr's fifth solo album, The Age of Everything, which is scheduled for October release.

Marr first rose to prominence as the guitarist and co-songwriter of The Smiths, the Manchester-formed rock band that operated from 1982 to 1987. Alongside vocalist Morrissey, Marr crafted the songwriting partnership that would define the band's sound and help establish The Smiths as one of the most important British acts of their era and pioneers of 1980s independent music. The group's original lineup also included bassist Andy Rourke and drummer Mike Joyce.

Since The Smiths' dissolution, Marr has maintained an active presence in music, performing with numerous bands and building an extensive solo career across multiple decades. title: Watch Van Halen’s Michael Anthony Play ‘Runnin’ With The Devil’ With Jason Bonham
summary: It was the first time in the 16-year history of Jason Bonham's Led Zeppelin Evening that a song not found in the Zeppelin catalog was performed at one of their shows
whatHappening: Michael Anthony, bassist for Van Halen, performed 'Runnin' With The Devil'—a Van Halen classic—alongside Jason Bonham at one of Bonham's Led Zeppelin tribute shows. It marked a historic first: the 16-year-old Led Zeppelin Evening had never featured a song outside the Zeppelin catalog until this performance.
whoInvolved: Michael Anthony is the bassist for Van Halen, the legendary American rock band formed in Pasadena in 1972 and credited with restoring hard rock to mainstream prominence. Jason Bonham is the son of John Bonham, Led Zeppelin's original drummer, and has spent 16 years headlining the Led Zeppelin Evening, a tribute show celebrating his father's legendary band.
whyMatters: The performance represents a rare departure from the strict setlist boundaries that have defined Jason Bonham's Led Zeppelin Evening for nearly two decades, signaling a willingness to expand the show's scope. It also underscores the shared musical DNA between Van Halen and Led Zeppelin, two foundational acts in rock history whose combined influence shaped generations of musicians.
articleBody:
Michael Anthony brought a piece of Van Halen's catalog to Jason Bonham's Led Zeppelin Evening when he joined the tribute show to perform 'Runnin' With The Devil,' marking a watershed moment in the 16-year history of Bonham's traveling exhibition of his father's legendary material. According to Rolling Stone, the performance was the first time a song outside the Led Zeppelin catalog had been featured at one of these events.

Jason Bonham has spent the better part of two decades curating these shows as a celebration of his father, John Bonham, who was the drummer for Led Zeppelin from the band's 1968 formation in London through their 1980 dissolution. Led Zeppelin, comprising vocalist Robert Plant, guitarist Jimmy Page, bassist and keyboardist John Paul Jones, and John Bonham on drums, pioneered the synthesis of heavy electric rock with blues and folk influences that became the template for hard rock and heavy metal itself. Their cultural footprint remains immense—they are among the best-selling music artists of all time.

Van Halen, formed in Pasadena, California in 1972, carved out their own towering legacy by restoring hard rock to the forefront of the music scene during an era when the genre needed reinvention. The band became known for electrifying live performances and the virtuosic guitar work of Eddie Van Halen, whose technical innovations influenced countless players. 'Runnin' With The Devil,' one of Van Halen's signature tracks, represents the hard-hitting energy and musicianship that defined their career.

Michael Anthony's appearance at the Led Zeppelin Evening underscores an implicit kinship between the two bands. Both Van Halen and Led Zeppelin occupied the upper echelon of rock's power hierarchy, commanding massive audiences and shaping the sound of their respective eras. By stepping onto the stage to perform Van Halen material within the framework of Bonham's tribute, Anthony created a symbolic convergence of two lineages that, while distinct in style, share common roots in blues-inflected hard rock and virtuoso musicianship.

The decision to break the Led Zeppelin-only tradition suggests that Jason Bonham may be open to occasional guest appearances and musical detours that honor the broader rock pantheon while maintaining the show's primary focus. articleBody:

The 2026 cancellation represents a significant step back for touring plans that had presumably been in development. Rather than risk further complications, Michaels is prioritizing his physical well-being and committing to a longer recovery timeline. whatHappening: ZZ Top returned to the stage in Austin for their first performance since the death of drummer Frank Beard earlier this week. Billy Gibbons told the crowd they were gathered for a celebration, signaling the band's determination to honor their late bandmate by continuing to perform.
whoInvolved: ZZ Top is an iconic American rock band formed in Houston in 1969, consisting of vocalist-guitarist Billy Gibbons, drummer Frank Beard, and bassist-vocalist Dusty Hill until Hill's death in 2021. Beard, who passed away in 2026 after five decades with the band, was a cornerstone of their signature blues-based sound.
whyMatters: Beard's death marks a watershed moment for one of rock's most enduring acts, bringing an end to an era of nearly uninterrupted lineup stability spanning five decades. The band's immediate return to performing signals their commitment to their legacy and fanbase, even as they face the challenge of continuing without a founding member.
articleBody:
ZZ Top played their first show since the death of drummer Frank Beard, taking the stage in Austin as Billy Gibbons addressed the crowd with a message of unity and remembrance. "We're all here for a celebration, you know what's going on. So we're gonna have a good time," Gibbons told the audience, according to Rolling Stone, setting the tone for a performance dedicated to honoring their late bandmate.

Beard's passing this week marked the end of an extraordinary chapter in rock history. The drummer had been with ZZ Top since the band's formation in Houston, Texas, in 1969, making him a foundational element of their sound for nearly five decades. Along with bassist-vocalist Dusty Hill, Beard formed the rhythm section that anchored Billy Gibbons' distinctive blues-influenced guitar work, helping ZZ Top develop the signature sound that made them one of rock's most recognizable acts.

The band's lineup had remained remarkably stable throughout their career until recent years. Dusty Hill's death in 2021 was the first significant change to the trio's composition, and Beard's death in 2026 represents the loss of the final surviving founding member alongside Gibbons. The drummer was known not only for his technical contributions but also for being an integral part of the band's visual identity and stage presence.

ZZ Top built their reputation over decades on a foundation of live performances, sly and humorous lyrics, and a carefully cultivated image that became iconic in rock culture. Beard's role as the "dear drummer," as he was affectionately referred to, was essential to the chemistry that made their concerts legendary. His passing leaves Gibbons navigating the future of the band at a pivotal moment.

By returning to Austin so quickly after Beard's death, ZZ Top demonstrated their commitment to their fans and their legacy. For longtime fans and the Austin community where the band originated, this performance represented both a time of grief and a reaffirmation of the enduring impact of ZZ Top's music.

title: Janie Bradford, Motown Songwriter Who Co-Wrote ‘Money (That’s What I Want’), Dead at 87
summary: "Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown," Berry Gordy writes in tribute to label's receptionist-turned-hit songwriter
whatHappening: Janie Bradford, the pioneering Motown songwriter and receptionist who co-wrote the enduring hit 'Money (That's What I Want)', has died at 87. Berry Gordy, Motown's founder, paid tribute to her as a foundational figure in the label's early history.
whoInvolved: Janie Bradford was an American songwriter who rose from receptionist to hit-maker at Motown Records, the Detroit-based label founded by Berry Gordy Jr. in 1959. Bradford's most famous collaboration with Gordy, 'Money', became a standard recorded by artists including Barrett Strong, The Beatles, and The Rolling Stones.
whyMatters: Bradford's death marks the passing of a key architect of Motown's sound during its formative years, when the label was establishing itself as a powerhouse of American popular music. Her songwriting legacy, particularly 'Money', has endured across generations and genres, influencing rock, pop, and soul music for over six decades.
articleBody:
Janie Bradford, a songwriter who helped shape Motown Records' golden era and co-wrote one of popular music's most recorded songs, has died at 87. Berry Gordy, the legendary founder of Motown, paid homage to Bradford's irreplaceable role in the label's creation, writing that "Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown."

Bradford began her career at Motown as a receptionist, a position that placed her at the heart of the nascent label during its earliest days. Founded by Gordy as Tamla Records on January 12, 1959, and incorporated as Motown Record Corporation on April 14, 1960, the Detroit-based operation was still finding its footing when Bradford joined. Her ascent from front-desk duties to songwriter reflects both her talent and the fluid, entrepreneurial environment Gordy cultivated at the label whose name became synonymous with Detroit itself.

Bradford's most enduring contribution to music came through her collaboration with Gordy on "Money (That's What I Want)." Originally recorded by Barrett Strong, the song became a template for what Motown would become: a bridge between rhythm and blues and mainstream pop. According to Rolling Stone, the track's infectious groove and straightforward lyrical hook made it irresistible to artists across genres. The song entered the rock canon when The Beatles recorded it for their second album, "With The Beatles," and it also appeared on The Rolling Stones' first UK EP, cementing its status as a standard.

What made "Money" remarkable was its staying power. Decades after its initial release, the song continued to be recorded and reimagined by successive generations of musicians, a testament to both Bradford and Gordy's songwriting acumen. The track transcended the soul and R&B markets where it originated, becoming a touchstone in rock and pop music—a rare achievement that underscored Bradford's gift for crafting hooks and narratives that resonated across audiences.

Bradford's career at Motown reflected a broader pattern within the label: talented individuals found opportunities to grow and contribute across multiple roles. While she may not have achieved the household-name status of some Motown artists, her influence rippled through the label's output and, by extension, through popular music itself. Her presence during Motown's formative period made her a custodian of the label's creative spirit during the years when it was establishing the sound that would define a generation.

With Bradford's passing, the music world loses one of the few remaining figures who witnessed and shaped Motown's transformation from a local Detroit operation into a global force in popular music.

Rodrigo's career trajectory has encompassed both music and acting. whyMatters: The incident highlights the dangers inherent in touring life for musicians and raises awareness about highway safety involving large vehicles. While the band escaped injury, the fatality among other motorists underscores the serious consequences of multi-vehicle collisions.
articleBody:
Buckcherry's tour bus was involved in a multi-vehicle accident that resulted in a fatality, though all band members aboard escaped without injury. Buckcherry, the American hard rock outfit from Anaheim, California, has maintained an active touring schedule since their 2005 reformation. Originally formed in 1995, the band dissolved in 2002 after releasing two albums—their self-titled debut in 1999 and Time Bomb in 2001. Lead vocalist Josh Todd and lead guitarist Keith Nelson revived the band in 2005 and released a new album in 2006 titled 15, which featured their biggest crossover success, "Crazy Bitch," and marked a significant moment in their career resurgence.

Tour bus accidents, while relatively uncommon given the volume of touring that occurs across the music industry, carry particular gravity due to the number of people typically aboard and the scale of the vehicles involved. articleBody:

title: Tupac Jurors See Keffe D’s First Public Interview About Killing: ‘I Got Cancer…Nothing Else to Lose’
summary: The jury also heard Keffe claim in a 2009 police interview that alleged gunman Orlando Anderson “peed on his hands” after the shooting to wash away gunpowder
whatHappening: Jurors in the Tupac Shakur murder trial are hearing testimony from Keffe D, a key witness who has now given his first public interview detailing his account of the 1996 killing. In a 2009 police interview played for the court, Keffe D claims that alleged gunman Orlando Anderson used an unusual method to dispose of evidence after the shooting.
whoInvolved: Keffe D is a witness in the case involving the murder of Tupac Shakur, the influential rapper and activist who was shot in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, in Las Vegas. Orlando Anderson is identified as the alleged gunman in the case that has remained unsolved for nearly three decades.
whyMatters: This testimony represents a major development in one of hip-hop's most infamous unsolved murders, offering potential breakthrough evidence after 28 years. The trial outcome could finally provide closure to Tupac's family and fans while setting a significant precedent for cold-case prosecution in high-profile crimes.
articleBody:
Jurors in the long-awaited trial over Tupac Shakur's 1996 murder are now seeing evidence from Keffe D, a witness whose testimony may finally shed light on one of the music industry's most enduring mysteries. According to Rolling Stone, the jury heard a 2009 police interview in which Keffe D claims that alleged gunman Orlando Anderson engaged in an unusual attempt to cover his tracks immediately after the shooting—specifically, that Anderson "peed on his hands" to wash away gunpowder residue.

On September 7, 1996, at 11:15 p.m., Tupac Shakur, then 25 years old, was struck by four rounds from a .40-caliber Glock 22 pistol in a drive-by shooting at a Las Vegas intersection. The shots hit Shakur twice in the chest, once in the arm, and once in the thigh. Suge Knight, the driver of Shakur's vehicle, was grazed by a bullet during the attack. Shakur died six days later from his injuries, and the case went cold for nearly three decades.

Keffe D's willingness to testify publicly now appears tied to his health. In the interview, he reportedly stated "I got cancer… nothing else to lose," suggesting that his terminal diagnosis has motivated him to finally speak openly about the circumstances of the shooting. This kind of deathbed confession or late-life testimony has occasionally broken open cold cases where witnesses previously feared retaliation or other consequences.

The specificity of Keffe D's account—including the detail about Anderson's method of attempting to remove gunpowder evidence—provides investigators with forensic and behavioral details that could corroborate or contradict other evidence presented in the trial. Such granular testimony is often crucial in cases where decades have passed and physical evidence may have degraded or been lost.

Tupac Shakur was one of the most influential musical artists of the 20th century, a rapper and actor whose work addressed social injustice and the marginalization of African Americans, though he was also closely associated with gangsta rap. His death at 25 cut short the career of an artist who had already sold millions of records and established himself as both a cultural and political voice. The unsolved nature of his murder has cast a long shadow over hip-hop history, making this trial a potential turning point in a case that has remained open longer than most homicides.

Bonnaroo will not happen in 2027. According to Rolling Stone, the beloved Manchester, Tennessee, festival is taking what organizers describe as a "much-needed year off" next summer, marking an unexpected break in the festival's annual schedule.

title: Tupac Murder Trial: Jurors Hear ‘Secret’ Police Interview with Keffe D Admitting Role in Shooting
summary: Duane “Keffe D” Davis now says he lied to investigators during the meeting to gain leverage while facing a potential life sentence on drug charges
whatHappening: Jurors in the Tupac Shakur murder trial are hearing testimony from a secret police interview in which Duane "Keffe D" Davis admitted to a role in the 1994 shooting. Davis now claims he lied during that interview to gain leverage while facing potential life imprisonment on drug charges.
whoInvolved: Duane Davis, also known as Keffe D, is a figure connected to the decades-old murder of Tupac Shakur, one of the most influential rappers and cultural activists of the 20th century who sold over 75 million records worldwide. whyMatters: The trial represents a rare moment of potential closure in a case that has captivated the public for nearly three decades. articleBody:
Jurors in the murder trial related to Tupac Shakur's death are being presented with a recorded police interview in which Duane "Keffe D" Davis detailed his involvement in the 1994 shooting that killed the legendary rapper. According to Rolling Stone, Davis now claims he intentionally lied to investigators during that encounter, asserting that he provided the false admission to gain leverage in his own legal situation as he faced the prospect of a life sentence on drug charges.

Tupac Amaru Shakur, known by his stage names 2Pac and Makaveli, was an American rapper and actor who became one of the most influential musical artists of the 20th century. His murder on the Las Vegas Strip in September 1994 remained officially unsolved for nearly three decades, making it one of hip-hop's most persistent mysteries. Shakur's body of work addressed social injustice and political issues affecting African Americans, and he sold more than 75 million records worldwide, cementing his status as a cultural icon far beyond music.

The introduction of the secret interview recording into trial proceedings presents a complex evidentiary puzzle for jurors. On one hand, Davis appears on the recording admitting to a role in the shooting—a confession that could be viewed as highly incriminating. On the other hand, his current claim that he fabricated the admission to manipulate investigators creates reasonable doubt about whether any statements he made during that interview can be trusted. This contradiction places the jury in the position of determining not only what happened nearly thirty years ago, but also assessing the credibility and motivation of a key witness whose own account of his actions has fundamentally shifted.

Davis's assertion that he lied to gain leverage reflects a common defense strategy in criminal cases, where defendants or witnesses claim they made false statements under pressure or to achieve some tactical advantage. The drug charges Davis faced at the time of the interview add context to his potential motivation—with his freedom and future at stake, a calculated admission might have seemed a worthwhile trade-off. However, the very fact that he had motive to lie then raises questions about his current testimony and motivations as well.

The trial marks a significant moment in the long-stalled investigation into Shakur's death. For decades, the case languished as a cold file, with no arrests or convictions despite numerous theories and suspects. The decision to finally prosecute, based substantially on Davis's involvement and testimony, suggests that authorities believed they had finally gathered sufficient evidence to move forward. Whether the jury will accept Davis's current version of events or weigh his recorded admission as more credible remains to be seen.
